sentences.text: You must be Andy.
David, how you doing?
Very good, very good.
Nice to meet you.
Yeah, nice to meet you too.
Sorry about that, I just got caught in traffic, came back to my office.
No problem, no problem.
Well, it's nice to meet you.
I'm a sucker for some kind of marketing effort that you did.
It caught my eye and it seemed to be served the right message at the right, to the right person at the right time.
So I thought, hell, it's only 15 minutes.
I can spare 15 minutes.
So maybe I'll tell you why I reached out in the first place and then you can take the microphone.
How's that?
Yeah, that's great.
I'd love to know more about what you're doing.
Good.
Yeah, I mean, I'm a, I'm a marketing guy.
Nothing at the client side, but on the agency side.
So a lot of what I've done my entire career is provide research strategy, creative development to support clients in their acquisition efforts.
Generally, trying to acquire customers sometimes build awareness, but that's too soft for most of our clients, so they like to judge us by our return on investment, Roas, etcetera.
We do a lot of branding work, we do a lot of market research.
Increasingly we're doing more and more digital marketing.
And frankly, to this point in my career, I kind of view myself as an architect that loves to design houses.
So I've been very focused on working in the business, not on the business, and I think I want to continue to do that.
This is a way for me to fill my children's education account.
It's a way for me to put money into my retirement account and ultimately fund a lifestyle and a household.
I love it.
I wouldn't change a thing about it.
I'm not working that hard at it.
But it's managing to be profitable enough to bring a smile to my eye.
There is nothing exitable, there's nothing appealing to investors about this business.
At some point down the road, as ageism starts to kick in, which is famous, this industry is famous for being ageist.
I would like to have a business that on paper is exitable and sellable.
And so I'm building right now tackle box version a tackle box 1.11.2, which is really designed to the branding and marketing of trade shows, business events and exhibitions.
I plan on bringing on a board.
I plan on making this a legitimate business with the sole purpose of creating a income statement that is appealing to investors two, three, four years from now.
I've never built a business like that before.
I don't know.
I never paid much attention to anything other than how much money's in the bank account.
But I know investors are more sophisticated than that.
So they're going to want to know about monthly recurring revenue and average revenue per customer and gross margins and net margins.
And I'm just straight up, not a math guy, so I'm over my skis.
What I do know is I want to build this right from the start to make it appealing in the end.
Make sense?
It does, yeah.
Okay, brilliant.
So whereabouts are you now?
What's your current revenue and EBITDA margin, if you know it?
Yeah, I don't know the margin.
I know that I'm probably earning more than I would be if I would have stayed working at Leo Burnett or Ogilvy or draft.
So I'm happy with it.
And my hours are very.
Not that much.
I think we'll probably hit 500 or $600,000 in revenue this year, which might sound like not much, but the truth is all of our staff right now are contractors.
I've got one full time contractor and a bunch of part timers.
And between you and me, a lot of the grunt design work we outsourced to Brazil for like $12 an hour.
So I think we're low in revenue, but probably high in margin by almost any standard.
Okay, brilliant.
So you're looking to build this further before you exit.
So how can I help you at the moment?
Which of the marketing efforts really hit the right spot?
Well, this is.
Would you describe to me a little bit about yourself and your areas of expertise, how you provide value?
Yeah, sure.
So we're in an m and a advisory.
We work on both the buy and the sell side.
So we work with buyers and sellers.
All marketing agencies.
All of our clients are marketing agencies.
And if not, they're financial investors in that they could be private equity or private individuals that are looking to acquire marketing agencies.
We have a platform called agencies.
Co agencies is a marketplace for buyers and sellers of marketing agencies.
So both owners and buyers are using the space.

And then we also work on a one to many course and coaching, helping agency owners to get more value out of their business so that they get a better exit by, well, a couple of different areas, but improving the business, basically getting it to a point where sometimes it's just moving things around a little bit so you get better margins, but just putting the business in a position to either make acquisitions or sell at a higher multiple.
So we do those three things, buying, selling and coaching.
Wonderful.
Yeah.
I mean, the business, I'm currently running.
I don't know, it's.
It'll probably never, I never probably let it get to the point where it's a really sharp looking business on paper.
I think it's just a way for me to be happy doing something I love and earning more than I ever thought I would.
So that's, that's tackle box current, but tackle box 2.0, like I said, is going to be a different ballgame.
It's going to be, um.
I want to exit.
There's a lot of acquisition within the trade show industry right now.
There's a lot of appetite from big companies to buy little agencies.
I think one of our clients who I'm developing a statement of work for right now, would be a prime candidate to acquire us, but were kind of small beans.
I think if we get four clients within the trade show industry, well be sitting above a million in revenue.
So I think the harvest is going to come kind of easy, especially given how easy its come so far.
And the board members that Im bringing in, I dont know how to incentivize board members.
I mean I dont know how to build a proper business and thats, that looks good number wise and that's why we're talking.
Maybe you can help me now.
Maybe you just let me go run this thing and come to you and say, is now a good time to sell?
Is now a good time to sell?
Is now a good time to sell?
So what's your, what's your horizon look like?
What's the timeline that you're working towards?
Is it a ten year thing or a 20 year thing?
No, I don't think so.
I think maybe ten years at most.
I mean, my kids are finally to the age where I can go do some proper networking and I think the floodgates are going to open.
Quite honestly.
There's so many shitty little agencies run by people that don't have the pedigree that I have.
I mean, our close rate when getting clients in this industry is probably 75%.

The people that have the spending dollars, they want a new agency, and they want an agency run by someone thats ran the global Marlboro man campaign for six years and was in charge of arguably the most famous ad campaign in America for the past ten years.
I think theyre a little starstruck, honestly, and that makes them predisposed to hire us.
And I'm pretty good at sales once I get in front of people that it seems to work pretty well.
Yeah.
So well you're right.
I think the first thing is, if you're not ready to sell for another five years, you probably are not under that much pressure to build the business.
But obviously there are ways to do that.
And I guess we could probably help you once you get to the point of around 1 million plus in revenue in terms of selling.
I mean, there is always a buyer for every type of business.
The way that we work is just trying to hit as many potential buyers as possible in the shortest space of time.
Because if you're ready to sell, somebody else is ready to buy.
We can get all those people at the table to discuss, and it's just down to personalities and chemistry whether we can get a deal done, really.
But there's always a buyer.
A lot of sellers I speak to feel that they're too small or somebody's told them they need to be at 5 million or you need to be at XYZ.
And it's not really true.

There are obviously more buyers for certain types of businesses, but there are plenty of solopreneurs out there with an SBA lender that's willing to give them the money that they need to acquire a one man business with a bunch of contractors.
So there are buyers for everything.
Then.
It's interesting.
It's interesting.
Yeah.
And then.
But again, you know, you want to get the kids through university or whatever it is that the plan is, or whatever the plan is.
You know, you.
You really just need to focus on what that exit number looks like and get into that.
Yeah.
And I will have business partners, at least one in this new venture, which is also unfamiliar territory to me.
And so, I don't know, I reached out.
Maybe you could talk about your coaching and how that works and who's right for that.
Or maybe I'll call you back when I'm 100 million in revenue or.
Sorry.
Well, yes, I'll be happy.
Hopefully, the business sells itself at that price.
I won't need you, but.
No, you'd be surprised, actually.
Yeah.
Okay.
Okay.
Anyway, if you want me to get revenue to a million, give me a couple years and I'll reach back out.
Your call.
Yeah.
So the coaching really is for agency owners, probably, that are at the point where.
Or they're slightly before the point where they're able to make acquisitions.
I see.
Or they're looking to sell, usually within the next twelve to 24 months.
So that's.
That's where we're helping agency owners the most when it's sort of early days.
It sounds like the track record that you've got.
You're able to go out and find investors to build this 2.0 version of tackle box.
I would say you probably need to build that first before we could help.
We will come in at the point where you can already see the horizon approaching, whether three to five year horizon is something you're building towards.
And what we can help do is bring that closer quicker to sort of a two year instead of having to wait three to five.

Everybody we speak to, basically apart from you, the majority of people we speak to are saying, you know, they want to, they want to, or they feel they're going to be ready to do their exit in three to five years.
So we're really helping those people bring that three year horizon closer.
Twelve months or 24 months, that's our focus.
Well, let's table this then.
Hopefully I come back at you with better looking bottom line or top line.
Never understood the difference, frankly, and let's do that.
If you have any kind of resources or links or anything to like what makes an agency economically appealing to investors, feel free to send those freebies my way.
But if not, that's okay, too.
Yeah, I will do.
I'll have a look through the stuff that we've got and the stuff that's relevant, but, yeah.
Great to meet you, David.
Sounds exciting, whatever it is you're building.
So thank you.
I'm very proud of it.
Probably never been more satisfied professionally in my career as I am now.
And part of me is like, if it ain't broke, don't fix it.
Um, but I think when the kids get older, I'm going to have more time to make this 2.0.
So.
Yeah, well, I would advise you not to change it.

Too many people are sort of scrabbling around for something that they don't, they don't need or want, really, you know, beating themselves up that they need to build a big business because that's what everybody's talking about on the Internet and actually you just need to build something that makes you happy.
Yeah.
And frankly, if this new business can't be run by the team, like, I just want to be light, I'm not going to be into it up.
Like, if I have to be up into it up to my neck, I'm going to crush it.
I don't, you know.
All right.
Taking enough for your time.
Thank you, sir.
Yeah, keep me in your network.
I'm sure we will need to have a discussion at some point.
All right, that sounds good.
Thank you, sir.
Great.
Have a great day and enjoy your weekend.
Speak soon.

summary.action_items:
**David Kelbaugh**
Build Tackle Box 2.0 to reach $1 million+ in revenue (03:37)
Reach out to Andy when revenue approaches $1 million (11:32)
Consider contacting Andy when closer to a 3-5 year exit horizon (12:52)

**Andy Day**
Send resources on what makes an agency economically appealing to investors (13:25)
summary.overview: In a recent exploratory business consultation meeting between marketing professional David Kelbaugh and M&A advisor Andy Day, they discussed the development of David's new venture, "Tackle Box 2.0," which aims to enhance branding and marketing for trade shows and exhibitions. David's current business is on track to generate $500,000 to $600,000 in revenue, but he seeks to make Tackle Box 2.0 a more attractive option for investors to achieve an eventual sale in 2-4 years. Andy highlighted his expertise in helping agency owners increase their business value for successful exits and suggested focusing on exit strategies rather than rigid revenue targets. Both agreed on the importance of leveraging David’s industry experience and fostering the right partnerships, while David committed to building Tackle Box 2.0 to surpass $1 million in revenue and reconnecting with Andy as he approaches that milestone. Andy will provide resources to help David understand what makes an agency appealing to potential investors.
summary.short_summary: David Kelbaugh met with M&A advisor Andy Day to explore strategies for his new venture, Tackle Box 2.0, which focuses on improving branding and marketing for trade shows and exhibitions. David's existing business is projected to generate between $500,000 and $600,000 in revenue. He aims to make Tackle Box 2.0 attractive to investors, targeting an eventual sale in 2-4 years. Andy emphasized the importance of exit strategies over strict revenue targets and highlighted his expertise in increasing business value for successful exits. They both recognized the value of leveraging David's industry experience and forming strategic partnerships. David committed to achieving over $1 million in revenue for Tackle Box 2.0 and reconnecting with Andy as he nears that milestone, while Andy offered resources to help David understand investor appeal for agencies.
